name: Roger II and the Kingdom of Sicily
summary: Roger II was crowned King of Sicily by the antipope Anacletus II in 1130, unifying Norman Sicily, Calabria, and Apulia under one crown. His court at Palermo was uniquely multicultural: Arab administrators, Greek bureaucrats, and Norman knights served side by side; royal decrees were issued in Arabic, Greek, and Latin. The geographer Al-Idrisi produced his famous world map there in 1154, and Roger's court attracted scholars from across the Mediterranean.
outcomes: Roger II crowned King of Sicily 1130

_quarry.structural_significance: The Norman Kingdom of Sicily was medieval Europe's most cosmopolitan monarchy; its synthesis of Arab, Byzantine, and Latin cultures produced unique artistic and administrative achievements.

sources_used: Metcalfe, The Muslims of Medieval Italy
Loud, The Age of Robert Guiscard
